source_text: Aeque stationes nostras ut indictas, quasdam uero et in serum constitutas nouitatis nomine incusant, hoc quoque munus et ex arbitrio obeundum esse dicentes et non ultra nonam detinendum, de suo scilicet more. sed quod pertineat ad indictionis quaestionem, semel pro omnibus causis respondebo. nunc ad proprium huius speciei articulum, de modo temporis dico, de ipsis prius expostulandum, unde hanc formam nona i dirimendis stationibus praescribant. si, qua Petrus et qui cum eo ad horam nonam orationis templum introgressi leguntur, quis mihi probabit illos ea die statione functos, ut horam nonam ad clausulam et expunctionem stationis interpretetur? atqui facilius inuenias Petrum hora sexta capiendi cibi causa prius in superiora ad orandum ascendisse, quo magis sexta diei finiri officio huic possit, quae illud absolutura post orationem uidebatur. porro cum in eodem commentario Lucae et tertia hora orationis demonstretur, sub qua spiritu sancto initiati pro ebriis habebantur, et sexta, qua Petrus ascendit in superiora, et nona, qua templum sunt introgressi, cur non intellegamus salua plane indifferentia semper et ubique et omni tempore orandi tamen tres istas horas ut insigniores in rebus humanis, quae diem distribuunt, quae negotia distinguunt, quae publice resonant, ita et sollemniores fuisse in orationibus di-. uinis? quod etiam suadet Danielis quoque argumentum ter. die orantis, utique per aliquarum horarum exceptionem, non aliarum autem quam insigniorum, exinde apostolicarum, tertiae, sextae, nonae. hinc itaque et Petrum dicam ex uetere potius usu nonam obseruasse tertio orantem supremae orationis munere. haec autem propter illos qui se putant ex forma Petri agere, quam ignorant; non quasi respuamus nonam, cui et quarta sabbati et sexta plurimum fungimur, sed quia eorum quae ex traditione obseruantur tanto magis dignam rationem adferre debemus, quanto carent scripturae auctoritate, donec aliquo caelesti charismate aut confirmentur aut corrigantur. et si qua, inquit, ignoratis, dominus uobis reuelabit. itaque seposito confirmatore omnium istorum paracleto, duce uniuersae ueritatis, an dignior apud nos ratio adferatur nonam obseruandi require, ut etiam Petro ea ratio deputanda sit, si statione tunc functus est. uenit enim de exitu domini, quem etsi semper commemorari oportet sine differentia horarum, impressius tamen tum ei secundum ipsum stationis uocabulum addicimur. nam et milites numquam immemores sacramenti magis stationibus parent. itaque in eam usque horam celebranda pressura est, in qua a sexta contenebratus orbis defuncto domino lugubre fecit officium, ut tunc et nos reuertamur ad iucunditatem, cum et mundus recepit claritatem. hoc si magis ad religionem sapit Christianam, dum magis Christi gloriam celebrat, possum aeque serae stationis ex eodem rei ordine statum figere, ut ieiunemus ad serum expectantes tempus dominicae sepulturae, cum Ioseph postulatum detulit corpus et condidit. inde et irreligiosum est ante famulorum carnem refrigerari quam domini. sed hactenus haec ex argumentationum prouocatione commiserim coniecturas coniecturis et tamen puto fidelioribus repercutiens. uideamus, an aliquid tale nobis de uetustatibus quoque patrocinetur. in Exodo habitus ille Moysis aduersus Amalech orationibus proeliantis usque in occasum perseuerans nonne statio fuit sera? legum Naue debellantem Amorrhaeos prandisse illa die existimamus qua ipsis elementis stationem imperauit? stetit sol in Gabaon et luna in Aialon, stetit sol et luna in statione, donec ultus est populus de inimicis suis, et stetit sol medio caelo. ut autem accedebat in occasum et finem diei unius, non fuit dies talis retro et in nouissimo, utique tam prolixus, ut, inquit, exaudiret deus hominem, parem scilicet solis, instantem tam diu in officio, stationem etiam sera longiorem. certe Saul et ipse in proelio constitutus manifeste munus istud indixit: maledictus homo, qui ederit panem ad uesperam usque, dum ulciscar de inimico meo, et non gustauit totus populus eius, et tota terra prandebat. tantam autem deus praestitit auctoritatem edicto stationis illius, ut Ionathan, filius Saulis, quamquam ignarus ieiunationis in serum definitae gustum mellis admiserat, et forte mox de delicto sit traductus et uix per precem populi periculo exemptus. gulae enim licet simplicis reus fuerat. sed et Daniel anno primo regis Darii, cum ieiunus in sacco et cinere exomologesin deo ageret, et adhuc, inquit, loquente me in oratione, ecce uir, quem uideram in somnis initio, uelociter uolans appropinquauit mihi quasi hora uespertini sacrificii. haec erit statio sera quae ad uesperam ieiunans pinguiorem orationem deo immolat.
thought_title: Defending the late hour of station fasts
orientation: Tertullian is answering opponents who accuse his group's station fasts of being a novelty because they extend them until evening, and he now argues from Scripture and tradition that the ninth hour and even later are fitting for ending a station.
pass_a_gloss: Equally they accuse our station fasts as commanded, and some indeed set until late, under the name of novelty, saying that this duty also is to be performed from free choice and is not to be prolonged beyond the ninth hour, from their own custom, of course. But as far as concerns the question of the command, I will answer once for all cases. Now to the proper point of this particular kind, I speak about the manner of the time, first I must demand from them themselves, from where they prescribe this form of the ninth hour for ending station fasts. If, because Peter and those who were with him are read to have entered the temple at the ninth hour of prayer, who will prove to me that they performed a station on that day, so that he interprets the ninth hour as the close and discharge of the station? But rather you may more easily find that Peter at the sixth hour, for the sake of taking food, first went up to the upper room to pray, by which more the sixth hour of the day could be the end for this duty, which seemed about to finish it after prayer. Furthermore, since in the same commentary of Luke both the third hour of prayer is shown, under which, having been initiated by the Holy Spirit, they were considered drunk, and the sixth, at which Peter went up to the upper room, and the ninth, at which they entered the temple, why should we not understand, with the indifference of praying always and everywhere and at every time clearly preserved, that nevertheless those three hours, as more distinguished in human affairs, which divide the day, which mark off business, which resound publicly, were also more solemn in divine prayers? This the example of Daniel also persuades, praying three times a day, certainly through the exception of certain hours, and not of others than the more distinguished ones, from then on apostolic ones, the third, the sixth, the ninth. Hence therefore I will say that Peter also observed the ninth hour from rather old usage, praying third with the duty of the final prayer. But these things are for the sake of those who think they act from the pattern of Peter, which they do not know; not as if we reject the ninth hour, at which we also perform much on the fourth day of the week and the sixth, but because for those things which are observed from tradition we ought to bring a reason so much more worthy, as they lack the authority of Scripture, until they are either confirmed or corrected by some heavenly gift. And if you do not know anything, he says, the Lord will reveal it to you. Therefore, setting aside the confirmer of all these things, the Advocate, the guide of all truth, ask whether a more worthy reason is brought by us for observing the ninth hour, so that that reason should also be assigned to Peter, if he performed a station then. For it comes from the departure of the Lord, which although it ought always to be commemorated without difference of hours, nevertheless more impressively then we are bound to it according to the very name of station. For soldiers also, never forgetful of their oath, obey stations more. Therefore the pressure is to be celebrated until that hour in which from the sixth hour the darkened world performed a mournful duty for the dead Lord, so that then we also may return to joy, when the world also received back its brightness. If this savors more of Christian religion, while it celebrates more the glory of Christ, I can equally fix the status of the late station from the same order of the matter, so that we fast until late, awaiting the time of the Lord's burial, when Joseph brought the body he had requested and buried it. Hence also it is irreligious for the flesh of the servants to be refreshed before that of the Lord. But thus far I have engaged these things from the challenge of arguments, striking back conjectures with conjectures, and yet I think with more faithful ones. Let us see whether anything of this kind also pleads for us from the ancient records. In Exodus, that posture of Moses fighting against Amalek with prayers, persevering until sunset, was it not a late station? Do we think that Joshua, warring down the Amorites, lunched on that day on which he commanded a station to the very elements? The sun stood in Gibeon and the moon in Aijalon, the sun and moon stood in station, until the people was avenged of its enemies, and the sun stood in the middle of the sky. But as it was approaching sunset and the end of one day, there was no such day before and in the last time, certainly so prolonged, that, he says, God would hear a man, equal of course to the sun, pressing so long in duty, a station even longer than late. Certainly Saul also, placed in battle, openly commanded this duty: cursed is the man who eats bread until evening, until I am avenged of my enemy, and all his people did not taste, and the whole land was lunching. But God gave such great authority to the edict of that station, that Jonathan, the son of Saul, although ignorant of the fast defined until late, had admitted a taste of honey, and perhaps was soon brought to trial for the offense and scarcely freed from danger by the prayer of the people. For he had been guilty of gluttony, although simple. But Daniel also, in the first year of King Darius, when fasting in sackcloth and ashes he was making penitential confession to God, and while I was still speaking, he says, in prayer, behold a man, whom I had seen in dreams at the beginning, flying swiftly approached me about the hour of the evening sacrifice. This will be the late station which, fasting until evening, offers a richer prayer to God.

choices.why: Keeps the legal/commanded force of indictas, which is central to the opponents' charge of novelty.
Serum means late in the day, toward evening; 'until late' preserves the temporal extension being disputed.

choices.english: is not to be prolonged beyond the ninth hour
choices.why: Detinendum has the sense of holding back or keeping; 'prolonged' captures the opponents' rule about the time limit.
rejected: must not be kept past the ninth hour
should not be detained beyond the ninth

choices.why: Expunctio is a technical term for completing or canceling an account; 'discharge' keeps the military/accounting flavor tied to statio.
Pressura carries the weight of the station's discipline; 'pressure' preserves the physical and spiritual strain Tertullian intends.
Pinguis means rich or fat; the literal rendering keeps Tertullian's metaphor of a fast-fed prayer as a richer offering.

pass_b_english: They likewise accuse our station fasts as commanded—and some of them set until late—under the name of novelty, saying that this duty too should be performed by personal choice and is not to be prolonged beyond the ninth hour, following their own custom, of course. But as far as the question of commanding goes, I will answer once for all cases. Now to the specific point of this particular practice—I mean the question of time—I must first take issue with them about the source from which they prescribe this rule of ending station fasts at the ninth hour. If it is because Peter and those with him are recorded as entering the temple at the ninth hour of prayer, who will prove to me that they were performing a station fast that day, so as to interpret the ninth hour as the close and discharge of the station? Yet you could more easily find that Peter went up to the upper room at the sixth hour to eat, before praying, which would make the sixth hour the end of this duty, since it would seem to have been completed after prayer. Furthermore, since in the same commentary of Luke the third hour of prayer is also indicated—at which those filled with the Holy Spirit were considered drunk—and the sixth, at which Peter went up to the upper room, and the ninth, at which they entered the temple, why should we not understand that, while the freedom to pray always and everywhere and at every time remains entirely intact, those three hours were nonetheless more distinguished in human affairs—they divide the day, they mark off business, they resound publicly—and so were also more solemn in divine prayers? This is also suggested by the example of Daniel praying three times a day, certainly through the selection of certain hours, and no others than the more distinguished ones—the apostolic hours from then on: the third, the sixth, the ninth. From this, then, I would say that Peter observed the ninth hour from older custom, praying the third time as the final prayer of the day. But I say this for the sake of those who think they are acting from Peter's example, which they do not understand—not as though we reject the ninth hour, which we observe most fully on the fourth and sixth days of the week, but because for things observed from tradition we ought to give a more worthy reason to the extent that they lack scriptural authority, until they are either confirmed or corrected by some heavenly gift. And if you are ignorant of anything, he says, the Lord will reveal it to you. Therefore, setting aside the confirmer of all these things, the Advocate, the guide of all truth, ask whether a more worthy reason can be given among us for observing the ninth hour, so that this reason may also be assigned to Peter, if he was performing a station fast then. For it comes from the Lord's departure, which, although it ought always to be commemorated without distinction of hours, we are nevertheless more deeply bound to at that hour according to the very name of station. For soldiers too, never forgetful of their oath, obey station duty all the more. Therefore the fast itself is to be observed up to that hour in which, from the sixth hour, the darkened world mourned at the Lord's death, so that we too may return to joy when the world received back its light. If this savors more of Christian religion, while it celebrates Christ's glory more, I can equally fix the status of a late station from the same order of events, so that we fast until late, awaiting the time of the Lord's burial, when Joseph took away the body he had requested and laid it to rest. From this it is also irreligious for the flesh of servants to be refreshed before the Lord's. But let me have done with pressing conjectures against conjectures from the challenge of arguments—and yet, I think, striking back with more faithful ones. Let us see whether anything of this kind from ancient times also supports us. In Exodus, was not that posture of Moses fighting against Amalek with prayers, persisting until sunset, a late station fast? Do we think that Joshua, when he was defeating the Amorites, ate lunch on that day when he commanded a station for the very elements? The sun stood still in Gibeon and the moon in Aijalon; the sun and moon stood still until the people avenged themselves on their enemies, and the sun stood in mid-heaven (Joshua 10:12-13). But as it was moving toward its setting and the end of one day—there was no day like it before or after—it was so prolonged, he says, that God heard a man, as though the sun were his equal, pressing on so long in duty, a station even longer by being late. Certainly Saul too, when he was set in battle, openly commanded this duty: Cursed is the man who eats bread until evening, until I am avenged on my enemy—and none of his people tasted food, and the whole land was eating (1 Samuel 14:24). And God gave such authority to the edict of that station that Jonathan, Saul's son, although ignorant of the fast defined until late, had tasted a bit of honey, and was perhaps soon brought to trial for the offense and barely rescued from danger by the people's prayer. For he had been guilty of gluttony, even if innocent. But Daniel too, in the first year of King Darius, when he was fasting in sackcloth and ashes and making penitential confession to God, says: While I was still speaking in prayer, behold, the man whom I had seen in dreams at the beginning, flying swiftly, approached me about the hour of the evening sacrifice (Daniel 9:21). This will be the late station which, fasting until evening, offers a richer prayer to God.

problems.source_quote: et si qua, inquit, ignoratis, dominus uobis reuelabit.
problems.why: The quoted Latin is not from Philippians 3:15; the citation is incorrect.
problems.fix: remove the erroneous citation or replace with the correct reference (e.g., 1 Cor 2:12 or the appropriate verse).
problems.ruling: Latin 'dominus uobis reuelabit' is not Phil 3:15; no such wording exists there. Citation is wrong and misleads the reader.

fixed: Removed the incorrect citation '(Philippians 3:15)'; the Latin 'et si qua, inquit, ignoratis, dominus uobis reuelabit' is not from Philippians 3:15, and no confident correct reference is identifiable from the source.

problems.quote: Therefore the pressure is to be observed until that hour
problems.source_quote: itaque in eam usque horam celebranda pressura est
problems.why: 'Pressura' means the pressing/fast itself, not 'pressure'; and it is to be observed until the hour of darkness, not 'that hour.'
problems.fix: Therefore the fast itself is to be observed up to that hour
problems.ruling: ‘Pressura’ means the fast, not ‘pressure’; rendering as ‘pressure … observed’ misstates the concept.

edits.old: Therefore the pressure is to be observed until that hour
edits.new: Therefore the fast itself is to be observed up to that hour

fixed: Changed 'pressure' to 'the fast itself' and 'until' to 'up to' to match 'pressura' (the fast) and 'in eam usque horam' (up to that hour).

problems.why: The vision described is from Daniel 10, not Daniel 9:3‑21.
problems.fix: cite Daniel 10:5‑6 (or the appropriate verses) instead of Daniel 9:3‑21
problems.ruling: Daniel 9:21 has the man Gabriel; the vision in sackcloth/ashes with 'man' flying is Daniel 10:5, not 9:3-21.

fixed: The vision of the man flying swiftly approaching Daniel at the hour of the evening sacrifice is from Daniel 10, not Daniel 9:3-21. The source words 'ecce uir ... appropinquauit mihi quasi hora vespertini sacrificii' correspond to Daniel 10:5-6, so the citation has been corrected.

fixed: Advocate: the brief's glossary already mandates 'the Advocate' for paracletus, and the English uses it consistently; no change needed.
a fatter prayer: source 'pinguiorem orationem' means a richer/fuller prayer; 'fatter' is too literal and odd in English, so changed to 'richer'.
Joshua 10:12-13: the English citation is correct for the sun standing still in Gibeon and the moon in Aijalon; no change needed.
1 Samuel 14:24: the citation is correct for Saul's curse; the phrase 'the whole land was eating' reflects the source's 'tota terra prandebat'; no change needed.
Advocate and Holy Spirit: the brief's glossary mandates 'the Advocate' for paracletus; the English already uses it consistently; no change needed.
fourth and sixth days of the week: the English correctly renders 'quarta sabbati et sexta' as the fourth and sixth days of the week; no change needed.
And if you are ignorant of anything, he says: the source 'inquit' refers to the Lord in the quoted Scripture (Philippians 3:15), and the English 'he says' is acceptable; no change needed.
Daniel 10:5-6: the source describes Daniel's vision in the first year of Darius at the evening sacrifice, which is Daniel 9:21-22, not 10:5-6; corrected.

problems.quote: the darkened world performed its mournful duty
problems.why: 'Mournful duty' is vague; context is the Passion darkness.
problems.fix: Render as 'the darkened world mourned' or 'performed its mourning'.

problems.why: Cited as Daniel 9:21-22 but the reference should be Daniel 9:21 only; v.22 is about Gabriel speaking.

last_rejected.ruling: Tertullian's 'quarta sabbati et sexta' means Wednesday and Friday; 'sabbati' is week, not Sabbath hour. English is correct.
